subject: How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects

messages.author: f11515f1564d7399
messages.subject: How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
parts: The Himalayan terrain is highly rugged and undulating, thus the straight line is not possible. The existing trails have been identified and planned for three days walk to count the macaques. However, planned to collect the data as per the distance framework., but since it is not the straight line, how to estimate the density of macaques?

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
parts:
Honnavalli

Methods for using line transect sampling with transects that curve has been examined in a 2001 publication by Hiby and Krishna

Hiby, L. and Krishna, M.B. (2001), Line transect sampling from a curving path. Biometrics, 57: 727-731. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00727.x

In short, if the paths are curved, as opposed to wiggly, standard analysis methods could be used with shortest distance between the animal and the path used as the "perpendicular" distance measure.  The challenge in the field is to measure this distance accurately.

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
parts:
Hi Kumara and list,

I expect you know this, but in case not: one thing to bear in mind since
you are planning to use paths is that if you do not follow random
transects (e.g., systematic random) placed within your study area then
there are two issues with using the data to estimate density.

First, macaque density in the vicinity of the paths may not be
representative of that through your study area of interest. For
example, paths tend to be on shallower ground but macaques may prefer
steeper ground. Also, macaques may be repelled from paths if they don't
like being close to humans. There are many other reasons why sampling
paths may not be the same as sampling random habitat, from the macaque
density point of view.

Second, if there is any kind of macaque density gradient going away from
the path (e.g., macaques may avoid being directly on paths, or the
opposite, they may like to use paths) then you cannot interpret the
pattern of detected distances as being about detectability, so you
cannot reliably estimate the detection function.

The first issue can be addressed to some extent by using the data
collected to build a model of factors affecting density (so called
"density surface modelling") but this is requires a good level of
training, and also if the transects completely avoid some habitats then
a reliable model is not possible. There are methods to deal with the
second issue also, which involve doing the survey in a slightly
different way (doing a series of points along the track and collecting
the angle to detected animals - this will only work if the density
change around the track is very local).

I appreciate that it may be impossible to survey anywhere other than
tracks. But I encourage you to consider the above issues and how much
of a problem they could potentially cause you. Perhaps for macaques
neither of these issues are big enough to affect inference unduly.

I'd be happy to discuss this further off the list if that would be helpful.

Best wishes, Len Thomas
